chunk_findings.detail: `depth` computes the number of ancestors between an item and its phase/root, then unconditionally truncates the result to 6. Depth is a property of well-formed input, not only of the malformed cycles the comment cites: for a phase `P` with a legitimate chain `P → t1 → t2 → t3 → t4 → t5 → t6 → t7` (each task's `parent` being the previous one), `closure`/`above` yields 7 ancestors, but `depth` returns `min(7, 6) == 6`. `board_rows` feeds that value straight into the markdown indentation and into the `"depth"` field of `board --json` (via `rows(...)`), so a task nested more than six levels below its phase is rendered at the wrong indent level (and reports the wrong depth in JSON). The whole point of this change is that the board must stay byte-identical while the tallies are recomputed in core; this new, silent cap changes the board for any hierarchy deeper than six, and the `min(..., 6)` is not what protects against cycles anyway — a parent cycle is handled by `closure`'s own visited-set (the `last.parent == last.id` term only reacts to a cycle that has already terminated), so the bound only ever bites legitimate deep nesting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/progress.py:depth (`return min(len(above) + (last.parent == last.id != root), 6)`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`progress.tally` is documented by the inline comment as counting at *every depth* ("the one phase rule: every depth, abandoned out"), i.e. it descends into sub-tasks of the tasks it is handed. The old code counted exactly the elements of `q.tasks_under(p.id)` (minus abandoned) and compared `n_done == len(tasks)`, and the `tasks`/`rows` list used for rendering is still taken directly from `under`. So when a phase has a nested sub-task, `n.live` and `n.done` no longer equal `len(tasks)` / `n_done`.

Concrete failure: a phase marked `DONE` whose direct tasks are all `DONE` but which has one nested sub-task still `RUNNING`. Old: `n_done == len(tasks)` is true, so the phase hits the `done += 1; continue` short-circuit and produces only a phase count. New: `n.done != n.live`, so the branch is skipped and a phase card is emitted, with `done`/`total` that include the nested task that never appears in `tasks`/`rows`. This changes `board --json`/markdown output for any hierarchy with nested sub-tasks, contradicting the stated invariant that those outputs must be byte-identical (this change is not in the list of the three permitted visible changes). The same divergence applies to `"done": n.done, "total": n.live` on non-done phases, where the card total can now exceed the number of rendered rows.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor drops the explicit non-empty guard that the old expression carried. Previously the test was `c := _phase_counts(items, p.id))[1] and c[0] == c[1]`, i.e. a phase was only "ready to close" if it had at least one live task child (`total != 0`) *and* all of them were done. The replacement is just `... and PR.phase_tally(st, p.id).complete`, and per the comment on the line above, `phase_tally` deliberately excludes abandoned tasks from the total. For a phase that is not DONE but has zero non-abandoned tasks — a freshly created phase, or a phase whose tasks were all marked ABANDONED — `phase_tally` yields `done == 0`, `live == 0`, so a `complete` predicate of the natural shape `done == live` evaluates to True. The progress line then appends `, N ready to close` for a phase that has nothing left to close, whereas the old code suppressed it (the `c[1]` term was falsy). This is a fourth visible change, not one of the three intended ones (B01281f654e/Bb24939611d/B45b55be6a4), so the progress line is no longer byte-identical to before for any state containing an empty or fully-abandoned phase. The every-depth counting intended by Bb24939611d is achieved by `phase_tally`'s recursion; the non-empty guard it replaced needs to be preserved (or `Tally.complete` must be defined as `live > 0 and done == live`) to avoid the spurious "ready to close".

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own rule block states that a phase's tasks are its *live* tasks and that "an abandoned task is SETTLED, not outstanding", so a phase cannot close only "while any of them is open". With `complete = self.live > 0 and self.done == self.live`, a phase whose every task is abandoned yields `Tally(done=0, live=0, abandoned=N)` and therefore `complete is False` — even though no live task is open, exactly the situation the rule says is settled. Concretely, `tally([t_state == ABANDONED])` returns `Tally(0, 0, 1)` and `Tally(0, 0, 1).complete` is `False`, so any consumer using `complete` to render a phase as done/ready-to-close (phase list / progress line) will keep such a phase open forever. The `live > 0` guard conflates "no live work left" with "never had any work"; dropping the guard (testing `done == live` directly) would make an all-abandoned phase settle as the rule describes.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old expression pinned the emitted order to `_ORDER = (DONE, RUNNING, REVIEW, OPEN, BLOCKED, ABANDONED)`:
`[{"state": s, "n": counts[s]} for s in _ORDER if counts[s]]`. The new one iterates `counts.items()`, i.e. whatever order `progress.state_counts()` happens to produce. Nothing in the diff guarantees that order. A natural implementation (`{}` built in first-encountered order, or `collections.Counter`) emits states in task-encounter order, not the canonical `_ORDER`. Concrete case: a project whose only two tasks appear in the store as RUNNING then DONE yields `task_counts == [{"state": RUNNING, ...}, {"state": DONE, ...}]`, whereas before it was `[{"state": DONE, ...}, {"state": RUNNING, ...}]`. `status --json` is then no longer byte-identical to the golden, and this is not one of the three allowed visible changes (phase list, progress sub-task depth, progress phase name).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_status.py:_data (`task_counts`)

chunk_findings.detail: `counts[DONE]` used to be unconditionally safe: `counts = {s: sum(...) for s in _ORDER}` always created a `DONE` key. The replacement `progress.state_counts(tasks)` has no such contract stated anywhere; if it returns only the states that actually occur (the obvious `Counter(t.state for t in tasks)` shape), then any project with zero completed tasks makes `counts[DONE]` raise `KeyError`, crashing the `status` export. Input that demonstrates it: `tasks` containing only RUNNING/OPEN tasks (or an empty project) -> `state_counts` has no `DONE` entry -> `KeyError: DONE` on this line. Note the retained `if n` filter on `task_counts` is exactly the "drop zero counts" behaviour that suggests zero entries are otherwise present, but the subscript on the very next statements assumes they are present for `DONE` — the two assumptions conflict unless `state_counts` materialises every state.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor replaces `epoch(r["at"])` (from `core.progress`) with `clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local")`, i.e. it newly asserts that naive timestamps be interpreted in the host's local zone. This is a semantic change, not a formatting one, so it is outside what `tests/test_clock_format.py` pins ("minute/date slices, age renderings, the now writers"). The run records it parses are written by `schedule.py`, which now stamps them with `clock.now_utc()` — a UTC instant — so their naive wall-clock text is UTC, and reading it back as *local* shifts every timestamp by the host's UTC offset. Concrete case: a run at 12:00 UTC stored as `...T12:00:00`, read on a UTC−05:00 host, becomes epoch for 17:00Z, i.e. `last` is 5 h too large; then `age_days = (now - last)/86400` is 5 h too small, so a cadence sitting on its period boundary is reported as *not* due, and for the due ones `since` renders a smaller `clock.fmt_age(now - last, "days", places=1)` value (e.g. "6.8 days" instead of "7.0 days"). Both the due/not-due decision and the rendered `since` string therefore differ from the pre-refactor output on any non-UTC host — the byte-identical guarantee fails, and no test in the formatting suite covers it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/operations.py (`clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local")`)

chunk_findings.detail: The original expression floored whole minutes: `f"{w['waiting_s'] // 60}m so far"`. The new call passes only the seconds and relies on `clock.fmt_age`'s default formatting. Compare the sibling migrations in this same diff: every place that reproduced a `secs / 60:.1f` rendering explicitly passes `places=1` (`cli.py` `held` and the attempt line). The lifecycle site is the only one that dropped its argument, and its old expression was a `// 60` floor, not a decimal/rounding format. If the helper's default does what the `places` parameter name implies — format `f"{s / 60:.{places}f}m"` with a default decimal count — the string is no longer byte-identical for any waiting time that is not an exact multiple of 60: with `waiting_s = 100` the old code emits `1m` (`100 // 60 == 1`) while `f"{100/60:.0f}m"` emits `2m`; with `waiting_s = 90` the old code emits `1m` while `f"{90/60:.0f}m"` emits `2m`. Changing `// 60` to a division-and-format helper silently replaces floor with rounding, so the "every output must stay byte-identical" contract is broken on this line unless `fmt_age` special-cases a floored default, which the caller does not request.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor does not just rename the helper: `epoch(r["at"])` (no keyword) became `clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local")`, which hard-codes how offset-less timestamps are decoded. The run timestamps in `runs` are written by the same clock helpers that write UTC (cf. `at = given or clock.now_utc()` in `schedule.py`, and the `%H:%M:%SZ` UTC rendering), so any log entry serialized without a `+00:00` offset — which the intent says must keep producing byte-identical output — is now interpreted in the process's local timezone rather than whatever the old `progress.epoch` default did. Concretely, with `TZ=America/New_York` and a run stored as `"2024-01-01T10:00:00"` (10:00 UTC), the decoded `last` moves by +5h (05:00 UTC), so `age_days = (now - last)/86400` is off by ~0.21 days; for a daily cadence near the `age_days >= days` boundary this flips the `due` verdict and also changes the `"since"` string emitted via `clock.fmt_age(now - last, "days", places=1)`. The format-pinning test `tests/test_clock_format.py` only pins rendering, not this decoding, so it would not catch the shift. The change is output-preserving only if the removed `progress.epoch` already defaulted to local; if its default was UTC (consistent with the rest of the module writing UTC), this is a regression.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/operations.py:_due (the `last = max((clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local") ...` line)

chunk_findings.detail: The old code inserted `lease.ttl_s // 60` directly into the f-string (`past its {lease.ttl_s // 60} min TTL`). For an `int` TTL this is an `int`, and the new code matches. But `clock.fmt_age` wraps the quotient in `int(...)`, whereas the old TTL expression had no `int()`. So for a non-integer `ttl_s` (e.g. a TTL read from config/JSON as a float), the rendered text changes: with `lease.ttl_s = 90.0`, the old line rendered `past its 1.0 min TTL` (`90.0 // 60 == 1.0`, formatted by the f-string), while the new one renders `past its 1 min TTL` (`int(90.0 // 60) == 1`). The same applies to any float TTL (e.g. `ttl_s = 600.0` → `10.0 min` becomes `10 min`). The `idle` and `ago` values are unaffected because their original expressions already applied `int(...)` (`int((now - lease.renewed_at) // 60)` and `max(0, int(... // 60))`), so only this third, newly-`int()`-wrapped TTL value is a behavior change. If TTLs can ever be non-integral seconds, the promised byte-identity does not hold.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:1029 (`ttl = clock.fmt_age(lease.ttl_s, "min")`)

chunk_findings.detail: The old `_now()` was a function defined in `rules.py` whose body called `datetime.now(UTC)` at *call* time. The replacement `_now = clock.now_utc` is a module-level **alias** that captures whatever function object `clock.now_utc` was at import time, so it no longer follows the `clock` module. Concretely: in an environment where time is frozen by replacing the clock (e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.core.clock, "now_utc", lambda: FIXED)` — or any production wiring that swaps the clock), `gates/runner.py`'s `compact_at` is re-imported and re-resolved per call and will stamp the frozen time into log filenames, while `rules._now()` keeps returning the real wall clock and writes real timestamps into the rule data, so two "now" writers in the same process disagree. This is also inconsistent with the way the other three sites invoke their helper (`clock.fmt_minute(...)`, `clock.iso_at(...)`, `compact_at()`) rather than pre-binding it. The fix is to keep a thin call-through (`def _now(): return clock.now_utc()`) or to call `clock.now_utc()` directly wherever `_now` is used.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/rules.py (`_now = clock.now_utc`)

chunk_findings.detail: The old expression was `f"... {w['waiting_s'] // 60}m so far"`, i.e. floor division that always yields whole minutes. It has been replaced with `clock.fmt_age(w['waiting_s'])`, dropping the explicit floor. For the two call sites that pass an explicit `places=1` the replacement is the same arithmetic (`secs / 60` formatted to 1 decimal), which shows `fmt_age` takes raw seconds and renders `seconds / 60` with `places` decimals. With the default `places=0` that is `f"{secs/60:.0f}m"`, which *rounds* rather than truncates. Given `waiting_s = 90` the old line printed `... 1m so far`, the new one prints `... 2m so far` (1.5 rounds to 2); given `waiting_s = 3599` the old line printed `59m`, the new one prints `60m` (59.983 → 60). Any caller/test that only exercises multiples of 60 (or only the `places=1` path) will not notice, but real `waiting_s` values are arbitrary, so the status output is not byte-identical to the old expression. To preserve the old string the call must floor before formatting (e.g. `fmt_age(w['waiting_s'] // 60 * 60)` or a floor/truncation mode), not rely on the default `places=0` rendering.

chunk_findings.detail: The old `_fmt_since` was a local `def`; the replacement is a module-level alias that binds the *function object* `clock.fmt_time` at import time rather than looking it up at call time. This is the exact defect that was confirmed and fixed for `rules._now = clock.now_utc` (finding 3): the project's tests/production wiring freeze or redirect time by swapping attributes on `ddflow.core.clock`, and a module-level alias silently keeps the original object. Concretely, `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.core.clock, "fmt_time", lambda t: "00:00:00Z")` (the same pattern the suite uses for `clock.now_utc`) followed by `reservations._reserved_msg(...)` still calls the pre-patch `fmt_time` and renders the real time-of-day, while every other refactored site in this diff (`brief.py`, `operations.py`, `schedule.py`) calls `clock.<helper>(...)` at call time and does follow the patch. It should be a `def _fmt_since(t): return clock.fmt_time(t)` (or an inline `clock.fmt_time` at the call sites), not an import-time alias.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/reservations.py:_fmt_since (`_fmt_since = clock.fmt_time`)

chunk_findings.detail: The previous review's item 4 is not answered by its probe, so I am re-raising it. The old expression was `f"... {w['waiting_s'] // 60}m so far"`, i.e. *floor division on the raw value*, and `//` on a float yields a float that the f-string renders with a decimal. Given `w['waiting_s'] = 119.9`, the old code renders `1.0m`; the new code renders `int(119.9 // 60)` → `1m`. Likewise `waiting_s = 3599.9` rendered `59.0m` before and `59m` now. The triage's probe does not refute this: it asserts `fmt_age(s) == f'{int(s) // 60}m'` for `s = 119.9, 3599`, but `f'{int(s) // 60}m'` is a restatement of the *new* function's behavior, not of the *old* expression (`f'{s // 60}m'`), which for those same inputs is `1.0m`/`59.0m`. So the test named "matches_every_old_rendering" compares the helper to itself and never demonstrates equivalence for non-integer input. Unlike the `ttl_s` refutation (which cited `ttl_s=int(...)` in `core/handlers/leases.py`), no evidence is given that `waiting_s` is always an `int`; if the API computes it via `total_seconds()` (or any non-int path) without truncation, the two renderings diverge exactly as shown, so the floor-vs-float difference is a real output regression that the probe does not address.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard is advertised as keeping "the expressions core.clock replaced" from growing back (`"""...A guard keeps the expressions from growing back elsewhere."""`, and the test is named `test_the_replaced_expressions_live_only_in_core_clock`), but `_BANNED` only covers two of the three replaced expressions: it bans the `fmt_minute` form (`\[:16\]\.replace\(...T...`) and `datetime.now(...)`, and never bans `fmt_date`'s replaced expression `ts[:10]`. Demonstration: appending `_x = "2026-10-07T01:02:03Z"[:10]` to e.g. `ddflow/services/rules.py` leaves `test_the_replaced_expressions_live_only_in_core_clock` green, even though the exact slice `fmt_date` was introduced to replace is now duplicated outside `core/clock.py` — i.e. the invariant the test (and module docstring) claims to enforce is false. (The same escape applies to a plain `[:16]` minute truncation written without `.replace("T"`, since the regex requires the `.replace("T"` suffix.) This is a test-only gap with no runtime impact, hence LOW.
